ourAnswer: (i) 3-(Chloromethyl)-2-(propan-2-yl)pentan-1-ol; (ii) 2,5-Dimethylhexane-1,3-diol; (iii) 3-Bromocyclohexan-1-ol; (iv) Hex-1-en-3-ol; (v) 2-Bromo-3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol

note: Parts (ii)-(v) agree exactly ((iii) differs only in the optional '-1-' locant). Part (i) is a BOOK PARENT-CHAIN ERROR, though both names denote the SAME molecule, HOCH2-CH(iPr)-CH(Et)-CH2Cl. The key selects a FOUR-carbon parent (butan-1-ol: CH2OH, CH, CH, CH2Cl) while a FIVE-carbon chain containing the carbinol carbon exists — CH2OH, CH, CH, CH2, CH3 — running through what the key calls the '3-ethyl' group. IUPAC requires the LONGEST chain containing the principal characteristic group, so the parent is pentan-1-ol and the name is 3-(chloromethyl)-2-(propan-2-yl)pentan-1-ol. Corroboration from the book itself: the exercise key's own answer to Ex 7.2(x) draws this same skeletal pattern with the FIVE-carbon chain as the parent, so the two halves of the book's own key are inconsistent with each other. No student is misled about the structure, only about which chain is the parent.

ourAnswer: (i) 1-methylcyclohexene; (ii) but-1-ene
keyAnswer: (i) 1-Methylcyclohexene; (ii) A mixture of but-1-ene and but-2-ene, but-2-ene being the major product, formed by rearrangement to the secondary carbocation
note: Part (i) agrees. Part (ii) is ours wrong: we named but-1-ene as the major product on an E2 argument. Re-derived, the key is right — loss of water from butan-1-ol cannot give a free primary carbocation, so a concerted 1,2-hydride shift produces the secondary butan-2-yl cation, which loses a proton to give the more substituted, more stable but-2-ene (Zaitsev). Our own authored _note had already named but-2-ene as the alternative and given exactly this mechanism, but the stated answer was the wrong one. Correct answer for (ii): a mixture of but-1-ene and but-2-ene, with BUT-2-ENE the major product.

keyAnswer: Eight lettered entries (a)-(h): pentan-1-ol; 2-methylbutan-1-ol; 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol; pentan-3-ol; 'Pentan-3-ol' again; 3-methylbutan-2-ol; 2-methylbutan-2-ol; 3-methylbutan-1-ol. Part (ii) is not answered.
note: The key lists EIGHT entries that cover only SEVEN distinct compounds, and PENTAN-2-OL IS ABSENT. Entry (e) is printed as 'CH3-CH2-OH-CH2-CH3' — an OH inserted INTO the chain, which is impossible as written (there is a separate OH drawn below on a bond) — and is labelled Pentan-3-ol, which is already entry (d). Read as intended, CH3-CH2-CH(OH)-CH2-CH3, it duplicates (d) exactly. The evidence is closed rather than circumstantial: the alcohols of C5H12O are a fixed set of eight, the key names eight items, two of them are the same compound, so exactly one real isomer is missing, and enumeration identifies it as pentan-2-ol, CH3-CH2-CH2-CH(OH)-CH3 (a secondary alcohol). Our answer lists all eight. Separately, the key does not answer part (ii) at all, so the primary/secondary/tertiary classification is unkeyed.

keyAnswer: (i) 1-Ethoxy-2-methylpropane; (ii) 2-Chloro-1-methoxyethane; (iii) 4-Nitroanisole; (iv) 1-Methoxypropane; (v) 1-Ethoxy-4,4-dimethylcyclohexane; (vi) Ethoxybenzene

TWO PARTS BREAK IUPAC LOCANT RULES, each denoting the same molecule under a non-preferred name. (ii) CH3OCH2CH2Cl: both substituents are prefixes and both numberings give the locant set {1,2}, so the tie is broken by citing the prefix that comes FIRST alphabetically at the lower locant; chloro precedes methoxy, so the name is 1-CHLORO-2-METHOXYETHANE, not the key's 2-chloro-1-methoxyethane. (v) the gem-dimethyl cyclohexane with a para ethoxy group: numbering from the gem-dimethyl carbon gives the substituent set {1,1,4}, numbering from the ethoxy carbon gives {1,4,4}, and {1,1,4} is lower at its first point of difference, so the name is 4-ETHOXY-1,1-DIMETHYLCYCLOHEXANE, not the key's 1-ethoxy-4,4-dimethylcyclohexane. Neither error misdescribes the compound.
